steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a high-level, conceptual walk-through of how a transformer works:

1. Token Embedding  
   • Each input token (word, subword, etc.) is mapped to a continuous vector.  
   • These embeddings capture basic lexical meaning.

2. Positional Encoding  
   • Since attention has no built-in notion of sequence order, a fixed or learnable positional vector is added to each token embedding.  
   • This tells the model where each token sits in the sequence.

3. Stacked Transformer Blocks  
   A “transformer” is essentially many identical blocks stacked one after another. Each block has two main sub-layers:

   a. Multi-Head Self-Attention  
     – For each token, the model computes “queries,” “keys,” and “values” via learned linear projections.  
     – Attention weights are computed by taking dot-products of queries with keys (across all tokens), then normalizing (softmax).  
     – Each token’s output is a weighted sum of all tokens’ value vectors, letting the model “attend” to relevant context.  
     – “Multi-head” means running this process several times in parallel with different projections, then concatenating the results.  

   b. Position-wise Feed-Forward Network  
     – A small two-layer fully connected network applied independently to each token’s representation.  
     – Introduces nonlinearity and allows each position to be transformed further.

   c. Residual Connections & Layer Norm  
     – Each sub-layer’s output is added back to its input (residual skip).  
     – A layer normalization step stabilizes and speeds up training.

4. Final Layer & Prediction  
   • After passing through all blocks, you have context-rich representations for each token.  
   • For language modeling, a linear+softmax layer predicts the next token or fills in masked tokens.  
   • For classification or other tasks, you pool or use special tokens (e.g., [CLS]) and feed into a task-specific head.

Key Advantages  
• Parallelism: Unlike RNNs, all tokens are processed simultaneously, making training efficient on modern hardware.  
• Long-Range Dependencies: Self-attention links every token directly to every other, capturing distant relationships without “forwards” or “backwards” recurrences.  
• Modularity: You can scale depth (more blocks) or width (more attention heads) to fit data and compute budgets.

That’s the core idea—layers of self-attention plus feed-forward transforms, bridged by residual connections, let the model learn rich, contextual representations of sequence data.
